summary: Engineered dissipation using a filtered reservoir that induces downward transitions in the instantaneous energy eigenbasis while keeping the ground state dark can accelerate adiabatic state preparation. This directional cooling mechanism improves runtime scaling from $\mathcal{O}(\Delta^{-2})$ to $\mathcal{O}(\Delta^{-1})$ in the strong-relaxation regime, with finite-temperature thermal excitations introducing an error floor that is surmountable when heating remains below target tolerance.
motivation: Adiabatic state preparation is limited by nonadiabatic leakage near small spectral gaps, requiring runtime scaling $\mathcal{O}(\Delta^{-2})$ to suppress excitation to error tolerance $\varepsilon$. Reservoir engineering suggests that carefully designed dissipation can stabilize useful quantum states; this work exploits this principle to remove nonadiabatic excitations as they are generated rather than requiring the system to avoid them.
method: A filtered Lindblad dissipator with engineered jump operators $K(s) = \sum_{m<n} \kappa_{mn}(s)|m(s)\rangle\langle n(s)|$ induces only downward transitions in the instantaneous eigenbasis, keeping the ground state dark. Effective two-level analysis near avoided crossings shows the quasi-steady excited-state population becomes $p_{\max} \approx \dot{\theta}^2/(4\Delta^2 + \Gamma^2)$, and finite-temperature effects including detailed balance are analyzed systematically.
result: Numerical simulations on transverse-field Ising chains ($N=10$, $J=1$, $h=0.3$, $\Gamma=3$) show the dissipative protocol reaches $P_{GS} \geq 0.90$ at substantially shorter annealing time than closed-system evolution; random spin-glass instances ($N=10$, $\Gamma=8$) averaged over 10 disorder realizations confirm the improvement persists despite disordered spectra. A superconducting-circuit implementation using structured multi-mode bosonic reservoirs and Purcell filtering is outlined to achieve the required asymmetric noise spectrum.
